title: A Comprehensive Treatise on the Amitayus Sutra (Aphorisms)
excerpt: Causing body and mind to gradually enter the Land of Bliss, gradually draw near to the Land of Bliss.

inline.s: Unremittingly steep yourself in the practice, and awaken to the meaning of the sutra,
deepening faith and vows, and practicing as it teaches.
Recite it often, listen to it often, remember it often, and practice it often,
causing body and mind to gradually enter the Land of Bliss and gradually draw near to the Land of Bliss.
The Land of Bliss is my home.

inline.s: Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand monks.

All these great sages had already attained the supernatural powers. Their names were: the Venerable Liaobenji, the Venerable Zhengyuan, the Venerable Zhengyu, the Venerable Dahao, the Venerable Renxian, the Venerable Ligou, the Venerable Mingwen, the Venerable Shanshi, the Venerable Juzu, the Venerable Niuwang, the Venerable Uruvela-Kashyapa, the Venerable Gaya-Kashyapa, the Venerable Nadi-Kashyapa, the Venerable Maha-Kashyapa, the Venerable Shariputra, the Venerable Maha-Maudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Dazhu, the Venerable Dajingzhi, the Venerable Maha-Juna, the Venerable Purnamaitrayani-putra, the Venerable Lizhang, the Venerable Liuguan, the Venerable Jianfu, the Venerable Mianwang, the Venerable Guocheng, the Venerable Renxing, the Venerable Xile, the Venerable Shanlai, the Venerable Rahula, and the Venerable Ānanda
, who were at their head.
There were also the Bodhisattva Universally Venerable, the Bodhisattva Manjusri, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of the Worthy Aeon, who all gathered at the assembly.

inline.s: There were also sixteen true men of virtue: the Bodhisattva Virtuous Protection, the Bodhisattva Good Reflection, the Bodhisattva Wisdom of Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Contemplator of Non-Abiding, the Bodhisattva Flower of Supernatural Power, the Bodhisattva Radiance and Splendor, the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, the Bodhisattva Root of Stillness, the Bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the Bodhisattva Jewel Splendor, the Bodhisattva Abiding in the Middle, the Bodhisattva Restraining Conduct, and the Bodhisattva Liberation, who were at their head.

All of them together reverently cultivated the virtues of the Great Being Universally Venerable, fully endowed with measureless practices and vows, and abiding within all the dharma-gates of merit. They roamed through the ten directions, employing expedient means, entering the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, and reaching the further shore in full.

They aspired to become Buddhas in countless worlds: forsaking Tusita Heaven, descending into the royal palace, abandoning the throne to leave home, and practicing the Way through ascetic discipline. They made these showings in order to accord with the world. With the power of concentration and wisdom, they subdued the devils and their grudges, attained the subtle Dharma, and realized supreme, right, and perfect enlightenment.

Devas and humans turned to them in reverence and asked them to turn the wheel of Dharma. Always with the Dharma-sound they awakened the worlds, broke through the fortress of afflictions, destroyed the moat of desires, washed away filth and defilement, and revealed the pure and bright. They tamed sentient beings, proclaimed the wondrous principle, stored up merit, and displayed the field of blessings. With the medicine of the Dharma they cured the threefold suffering. They ascended the stage of consecration, and conferred the prophecy of bodhi. As teachers of the bodhisattvas, acting as acharyas, they constantly practiced the boundless practices which accord with the teaching. They matured the boundless roots of virtue of the bodhisattvas, and countless Buddhas all together kept them in mind.

In all Buddha-lands they were able to manifest themselves. Like a skilled magician, displaying many different forms, yet within those forms nothing is truly obtainable. These bodhisattvas were likewise. They fully penetrated the nature of dharmas, and understood the characteristics of sentient beings. They made offerings to all Buddhas, and guided and opened up all living beings. Manifesting their bodies, like a flash of lightning, they shattered the net of demonic views and untangled all the bonds and entanglements. They caused them to far transcend the stage of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to enter the dharma-gate of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They skillfully established expedient means, and revealed the three vehicles.

Among the lowly and middling, they manifested nirvāṇa. They attained the samādhis that are beyond arising and ceasing, and all the dharanis. At the right season they awakened into the Flower-Adornment Samādhi, endowed with the complete retention of hundreds of thousands of samādhis. Dwelling in deep meditative concentration, they fully beheld countless Buddhas, and in a single instant of thought roamed throughout all Buddha-lands.

They manifested themselves as great beings, attained the Buddha's eloquence, and dwelt in the practice of Universally Venerable. They were able to distinguish the languages of sentient beings, to teach and transform with the display of the real and ultimate, surpassing all the dharmas of the world. Their minds constantly dwelt upon the Way of saving the world, and amid all things they were free and at ease, becoming the uninvited friends of all classes of beings. They upheld the Tathagata's deep treasury of Dharma, protecting the Buddha-seed so that it never ceased.

They aroused great compassion, pitying sentient beings, expounding the eloquence of kindness, bestowing the Dharma-eye, closing off the evil paths, and opening the gates of goodness. Toward all sentient beings they regarded them as themselves, rescuing, carrying, and taking them up, and bringing them all to the other shore. They all obtained the measureless merits of all Buddhas, with wisdom and sagely brightness beyond thought.

Such great bodhisattvas as these, measureless and boundless, gathered at that time. There were also five hundred nuns, seven thousand pure-hearted men, five hundred pure-hearted women, and the devas of the desire realm and the deva realm, all the devas and Brahma assemblies, all joining the great gathering.

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One's majestic radiance shone brilliantly, like molten gold gathered together, and again like a bright mirror, with its brilliance pervading within and without, shining forth a great light, changing into hundreds and thousands of transformations. The Venerable Ānanda thought to himself: Today the World-Honored One's body and faculties are joyful and pure; his radiant countenance is dignified, and his jewel-land is adorned. Since I have attended the Buddha, I have never seen him thus. I rejoice to gaze upon him, and a mind of rare wonder arises.

Then he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with hands pressed together, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you enter the great still concentration, abide in the extraordinary Dharma, abide in the conduct of the Guide to which all Buddhas resort, the most supreme path. Past, present, and future, Buddhas think of one another. Do you think of the Buddhas of the past and future? Do you think of the Buddhas of other regions in the present? Why do your majestic powers shine forth and auspicious radiances appear so wonderfully? We pray you will speak them.

Then the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: Excellent! Excellent! For the sake of pitying, benefiting, and delighting all sentient beings, you are able to ask this subtle meaning. This question of yours surpasses in merit offering to all the arhats and pratyekabuddhas in a whole world, and giving alms for many aeons to all the devas and people, and to the wriggling
xuan
flying and creeping
(ru)
creatures by a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand times. Why? Because the devas and people of the future, all life that has perception, will be saved and liberated because of your asking.
Ānanda, the Tathagata, with measureless great compassion, taking pity
jin

on the three worlds, has thus appeared in the world. He proclaims and illumines the path of the Buddha's teaching, wishing to rescue the multitude of the deluded, and to bestow upon them the benefit of the real and true. Hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing. This question you now ask brings much benefit.

Ānanda, you should know that the Tathagata's right and universal knowledge is immeasurable in wisdom and without obstruction. He can, in the space of a single thought, remain in the world for immeasurable billions of aeons, with body and faculties neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this so? Because the Tathagata's concentration and wisdom are perfect, flowing freely without limit, and he has attained the supreme freedom over all dharmas.
Ānanda, listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I will now explain it to you in detail.

The Buddha told Ānanda: In the past, a long, long time ago, in an immeasurable, inconceivable, countless and inexpressible number of aeons, the Tathagata Radiance of the Blooming Flower appeared in the world, teaching, transforming, and liberating countless sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then passed into nirvāṇa. Next there was a Tathagata named Radiant Light, next named Moonlight, next named Sandalwood Fragrance, next named King of the Good Mountain, next named Sumeru Celestial Crown, next named Sumeru Equal Radiance, next named Moon Color, next named Right Mindfulness, next named Free from Defilement, next named Without Attachment, next named Dragon Deva, next named Night Light, next named Peaceful Radiant Peak, next named Motionless Ground, next named Wondrous Jewel Flower, next named Jewel Golden Color, next named Jewel Treasury, next named Flame Radiance, next named Flame Root, next named Earth Seed, next named Moon Image, next named Sun Sound, next named Liberation Flower, next named Adornment Radiance, next named Ocean Awareness Supernatural Power, next named Water Light, next named Great Fragrance, next named Free from Dust and Defilement, next named Renouncing the Mind of Disgust, next named Jewel Flame, next named Wondrous Peak, next named Courageous Uprightness, next named Merit Holding Wisdom, next named Shielding the Light of Sun and Moon, next named Sun and Moon Jewel Radiance, next named Supreme Jewel Radiance, next named Highest Chief, next named Bodhi Flower, next named Moon Brightness, next named Sunlight, next named Flower Color King, next named Water Moonlight, next named Dispelling Ignorance and Darkness, next named Crossing the Obstruction of Purity, next named Pure Faith, next named Good Abode, next named Majestic Power, next named Dharma Wisdom, next named Phoenix Sound, next named Lion Sound, next named Dragon Sound, next named Dwelling in the World. Such Buddhas as these, all had already passed.
At that time, there was then another Buddha,

named Tathagata Free and Self-Masterful King of the World, worthy of offerings, right and universal knowledge, perfect in conduct and understanding, well gone, knower of the world, supreme teacher, tamer of men, teacher of devas and humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. For forty-two aeons he was in the world teaching, at which time he spoke the sutras and expounded the Way for the devas and the people of the world.

There was a great ruler named King of the Beneficent World, who upon hearing the Buddha speak the Dharma, rejoiced and comprehended, and immediately brought forth the mind of supreme, true Way. He relinquished his kingdom and abandoned his throne, and practiced as a monk, named Dharmakara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.

High in talent, brave and wise, he stood apart from the world; his faith, understanding, and clear mindfulness were all the foremost. Moreover, he had supreme practices and vows, and the power of mindfulness and wisdom, which heightened his mind firm and unmoving. In his cultivation, diligent and advancing, none could surpass him.
He went to the Buddha, bowed his head, knelt long, pressed his hands together in the Buddha's direction, and with verses praised the Buddha, bringing forth vast and great vows.
The verses said:

The Tathagata's subtle form is dignified and pure,
In all the world there is no equal;

His measureless light illumines the ten directions,
Sun, moon, and blazing jewels all hide their beams.

The World-Honored One can sound a single voice,
And beings each and all hear it as their kind;

He can reveal one wondrous body,
And cause all beings to see it as their kind.

May I obtain the Buddha's pure voice,
Whose Dharma-sound spreads to no boundary;

Proclaiming the gate of precepts, concentration, and vigor,
And reaching through the subtle and profound Dharma.

Wisdom vast and deep as the sea,
The mind within pure, free from all toil;

Surpassing the gate of endless evil paths,
Swiftly reaching the final shore of bodhi.

Ignorance, greed, and anger are forever gone,
Delusions ended and faults wiped away by samādhi's power;

So too, like the countless Buddhas of the past,
I am the great guide for all those beings.

Able to save all the worlds,
From birth, old age, illness, and death, from all their suffering;

Always practicing giving, precepts, and patience,
Vigor, meditation, and wisdom, the six perfections.

Those not yet saved I cause to be saved,
Those already saved I cause to become Buddhas;

Though one make offerings to sages as numerous as the Ganges sands,
It is not equal to bravely and firmly seeking right awakening.

May I abide in samādhi,
Forever letting forth light to illumine all;

May I attain a vast and pure dwelling,
Supremely adorned, with nothing to match it.

The classes of beings in the cycling worlds
Quickly be born in my land and receive peace and joy;

Always moving the heart of compassion to rescue sentient beings,
And exhausting the measureless beings in suffering.

My practice is determined with firm strength,
Only the Buddha's sage wisdom can perceive and know it;

Even should my body fall into all the suffering,
Such a vow of mind shall forever never retreat.

Having spoken these verses, the monk Dharmakara said to the Buddha: I am now on the bodhisattva path, and have already brought forth the mind of supreme right awakening, wishing to become a Buddha and be like the Buddha in all things. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the Dharma to me, and I will receive and hold it, practicing as it teaches, pulling out the root of all the hard toilsome birth and death, and swiftly attaining supreme right and perfect enlightenment.

I wish that when I become a Buddha, my wisdom and light, the land where I dwell, and the name of the teacher, all be heard throughout the ten directions. The devas and people, and the creeping and flying creatures, who come to be born in my land, shall all be bodhisattvas. If I make this vow to surpass the countless Buddha-lands, may it be attained?

The Buddha Free and Self-Masterful King of the World then spoke this scripture to Dharmakara: For example, if one man were to measure the great sea with a small ladle, passing through many aeons, he might still reach its bottom and obtain its wondrous treasure. If a person with utmost sincerity seeks the Way, being diligent and unceasing, he will surely attain the fruit; what vow could be unfulfilled?

You yourself should reflect: what expedient means must be cultivated to accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land? As to what practice to perform, you yourself should know. The pure Buddha-land, you yourself should take it in.

Dharmakara said: This meaning is vast and profound, beyond my reach. I pray only that the Tathagata, the right and universal knowledge, will broadly expound the measureless wondrous lands of the Buddhas. If I can hear such dharmas and reflect, practice, and cultivate, I vow to fulfill my wish.

The Buddha Free and Self-Masterful King of the World, knowing he was lofty and clear, with vows deep and vast, then spoke to him of the twenty-one billion Buddha-lands, with the characteristics of their merits, adorned, pure, vast, and perfect. According to the wish of his mind, he revealed them all to him. While speaking this Dharma, a thousand billion years passed.

At that time Dharmakara, having heard what the Buddha spoke, saw them all and brought forth the supreme, extraordinary vow. He reflected to the ultimate on the good and evil of those devas and people, and the coarseness and excellence of their lands. Then he single-mindedly chose what he desired, and formed the great vows.

Diligently and earnestly seeking, with respectful and careful holding, he cultivated merit, and fulfilled the practice for five aeons. In the matter of the merits and adornments of those twenty-one billion Buddha-lands, he understood and penetrated them clearly, as if one Buddha-land. The Buddha-land he took in surpassed them all.

Having taken them in, he again went to where the Tathagata Free and Self-Masterful King of the World was. He bowed his head at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, pressed his hands together and stood, saying: World-Honored One, I have already accomplished the pure conduct of taking in a Buddha-land.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Now just the time, you should speak it fully, causing the assembly to be joyful, and also causing the great assembly, upon hearing this Dharma, to obtain great benefit. Being able, in the Buddha-land, to cultivate and take in, you fulfill the measureless great vows.
Dharmakara said: I pray only that the World-Honored One, with great compassion, will hear and examine me.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be in my land hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 1: No Evil Destinies in the Land)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land, after their life ends, should fall again into the three evil destinies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 2: No Falling into Evil Destinies Again)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not all be full of true golden-colored bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 3: Bodies of True Golden Color)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should differ in form and color, having the ugly or the fair, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 4: Neither Ugly nor Fair)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not attain the supernatural power of knowing past lives, at least knowing the events of a hundred thousand billion nayuta aeons, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 5: The Power of Knowing Past Lives)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not attain the divine eye, at least seeing the hundred thousand billion nayuta Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 6: The Power of the Divine Eye)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not attain the divine ear, at least hearing what the hundred thousand billion nayuta Buddhas speak and not receiving and holding it all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 7: The Power of the Divine Ear)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not attain the power of knowing the thoughts of others, at least knowing the thoughts of the beings in the hundred thousand billion nayuta Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 8: The Power of Knowing Others' Thoughts)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not attain the power of psychic travel, in a single instant of thought unable to pass beyond the hundred thousand billion nayuta Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 9: The Unobstructed Power of Psychic Travel)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should give rise to thoughts of reckoning and be attached to the body, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 10: Not Being Attached to the Body)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not abide in the right and certain state, and certainly reach nirvāṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 11: Abiding in the Right and Certain State)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light should be limited, at least not illumining the hundred thousand billion nayuta Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 12: The Measureless Light)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my life should be limited, at least limited to a hundred thousand billion nayuta aeons, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 13: The Measureless Life of the Buddha)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sravakas of my land should be countless, such that if all the beings of the three thousand great thousand worlds became pratyekabuddhas and, for a hundred thousand aeons, together computed and counted them, they could know their number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 14: Countless Sravakas)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should have lifespans without limit, except for their own vows, with long or short at will; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 15: Measureless Lifespans of the Beings)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should even hear of any name of evil, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 16: Hearing No Evil Name)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countess Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions should not all praise and proclaim my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 17: Praise by All the Buddhas)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions should, with utmost sincerity, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, even with ten thoughts, and not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment; except only the five rebellious acts and slandering the right Dharma.
(Vow 18: Certain Rebirth through Ten Thoughts)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions should bring forth the bodhi mind, cultivate all merits, with utmost sincerity make vows, and desire to be born in my land, and at the end of their lives were it that I do not appear before them surrounded by the great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 19: Rebirth through Utmost Sincerity)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions, hearing my name, should think of my land, plant the roots of all virtues, with utmost sincerity direct their merit, and desire to be born in my land, and their wish not be fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 20: Certain Rebirth through Mindfulness)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land should not all be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 21: The Thirty-Two Marks)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands in other regions, coming to be born in my land, should not certainly reach the stage of one-life continuation; except for their own vows, for the sake of beings, to don the armor of the great vows, enter other worlds, and freely save and liberate them all; roaming in the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, accumulating the root of merit, making offerings to the Tathagatas of the ten directions; opening and transforming measureless beings countless as the Ganges sands, causing them to stand on the supreme and true Way, transcending the ordinary grades of the stages of practice, and presently cultivating the virtue of Universally Venerable; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 22: One-Life Continuation)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land, relying on the Buddha's power, should make offerings to the Buddhas, and in the time of a single meal be unable to reach all the measureless, countless billions of nayuta Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 23: Offering to All Buddhas)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land, in the presence of the Buddhas, should display their roots of merit, and the offerings they need should not be as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 24: Offerings as Desired)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land should not be able to expound the wisdom of omniscience, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 25: Expounding the Wondrous Wisdom)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land should have bodies sixteen yojanas tall, and all obtain the diamond bodily frame of narayana; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 26: The Body of Narayana)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land, and all the myriad things, should be adorned, pure, bright, and beautiful, with form and color extraordinary, reaching the utmost depth and subtlety, beyond any measure; and were it that any of the beings, even attaining the divine eye, could clearly understand and explain their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 27: All Things Adorned and Pure)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land, even those with but little merit, should not be able to perceive and know the tree of the enlightenment site with its measureless lights and colors, four million li in height, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 28: Knowing and Seeing the Bodhi Tree)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land, when receiving, reading, and reciting the sutra-dharmas, and holding, speaking, and propagating them, should not attain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 29: Wisdom through Reciting the Sutras)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas of my land should be measurable, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 30: Unmeasurable Wisdom and Eloquence)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land should be pure, and it clearly reveal and illuminate all the measureless, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, like a bright mirror in which one sees one's own face; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 31: Illuminating the Ten Directions)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground upward to the sky, the palaces, towers, and viewing galleries, the ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, all the many things in my land, should all be formed of boundless jewels and fragrance together, adorned and wondrous, surpassing the devas and humans, with their fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodhisattvas who hear it should all cultivate the Buddha's conduct; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 32: The Splendor of Jewel Fragrance)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, upon my light touching their bodies, should have body and mind become supple and gentle, surpassing the devas and humans; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 33: Supple Bodies Upon Touching the Light)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not attain the bodhisattva's patient acceptance of non-arising, and the various deep total retentions, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 34: Attaining Patience upon Hearing the Name)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, I should cause my land to have no women. The women of the other regions who desire to be born in my land should immediately become men. The measureless devas and humans, even the flying and creeping creatures, who come to be born in my land, should all be transformed in the lotus flowers of the seven-jeweled ponds, and when grown up should all become bodhisattvas and arhats; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 35: No Women, Transformed in Lotus)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, after the end of their lives, should not always cultivate the pure conduct until they reach the Buddha's path, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 36: Always Cultivating Pure Conduct)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not prostrate the whole body, bow their heads and pay homage, rejoice with faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, such that the devas and people of the worlds all respect them; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 37: Homage by Devas and Humans)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and people of my land, desiring clothing, should have it appear as soon as they think of it, so that, as the Buddha has praised, the appropriate and wondrous robes are naturally upon their bodies; if there should be need of cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 38: Wondrous Robes Upon Thought)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the enjoyment of the devas and people of my land should not equal that of a monk whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 39: Joy Like the Exhaustion of Outflows)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of my land, wishing at will to see the measureless, adorned and pure Buddha-lands in the ten directions, should immediately, as they wish, within the jeweled trees, see them all revealed, like a bright mirror in which one views one's face; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 40: Revealing the Lands in the Trees)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the other regions, upon hearing my name, should, until they attain Buddhahood, have faculties deficient and incomplete, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 41: Faculties Without Deficiency)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the other regions, upon hearing my name, should all attain the pure and liberated samādhi, abiding in that samādhi, in the space of a single thought make offerings to the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, without losing the concentration of mind; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 42: Abiding in Concentration and Making Offerings)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the other regions, upon hearing my name, after the end of their lives, should be born into a noble and honored family; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 43: Merit upon Hearing the Name)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the other regions, upon hearing my name, should rejoice, leap with joy, cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, and be endowed with the roots of merit; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 44: Endowed with the Roots of Merit)

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of the other regions, upon hearing my name, should all attain the universal and equal samādhi, abiding in that samādhi, until they attain Buddhahood, always seeing the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas; if it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 45: The Universal and Equal Samādhi)
If I attain Buddhahood, may the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their own vows, whatever Dharma they wish to hear, hear it spontaneously. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 46: Hearing the Dharma as Vowed)
If I attain Buddhahood, may the hosts of bodhisattvas in other lands, upon hearing my name, at once attain non-regression. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 47: Non-Regression on Hearing the Name)

If I attain Buddhahood, may the hosts of bodhisattvas in other lands, upon hearing my name, at once attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma immediately attain non-regression. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 48: Attaining the Three Patient Acceptances)
The Buddha told Ānanda: At that time, after the Bhiksu Dharmakara had proclaimed these vows, he uttered a verse:
I set a resolve surpassing the world to reach the supreme Way; if these vows remain unfilled, I vow never to attain enlightenment.
Again I make myself a great donor, giving relief to all in poverty and distress, that all these hosts of beings may know no sorrow or trouble through the long night.
I give rise to all roots of good and accomplish the fruit of bodhi; if I attain enlightenment, I shall take the name of Immeasurable Life.
Beings hearing this name will all come to my land, with bodies of gold like the Buddha’s, their subtle marks all perfectly complete.
With a heart of great compassion, I shall benefit all the many beings, and, detached from desire, in deep right mindfulness, with pure wisdom, cultivate the pure conduct.
May my wisdom-light universally shine upon the lands of the ten directions, dispelling the darkness of the three defilements, and clearly saving beings from all calamities.
All beings shall relinquish the suffering of the three evil paths, extinguishing the darkness of all afflictions, opening the eye of wisdom and attaining a body of light.
I shall close off every evil path and open the gate to the realms of good; for beings I shall open the treasury of Dharma and widely bestow the jewels of merit.
Like the Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom, I shall practice the conduct of compassion; I shall always be the teacher of gods and humans, and become the hero of the three realms.
I shall expound the Dharma with a lion’s roar, widely crossing over all sentient beings, fulfilling the vows made in the past, that all may become Buddhas.
If these vows are accomplished, the great thousand worlds shall be moved; the gods of the sky shall rain down wondrous and precious flowers.

The Buddha told Ānanda: After the Bhiksu Dharmakara had spoken this verse, at once the whole earth moved in six ways. Heaven rained wondrous flowers, scattering them over him; and spontaneously celestial music arose, while a voice in the sky proclaimed: “You shall surely attain supreme right enlightenment.”

Ānanda, after the Bhiksu Dharmakara had proclaimed these great vows before the Tathagata Lokesvararaja and amidst the assemblies of gods and humans, he abode in true wisdom, vigorously and earnestly advanced, and with single mind devoted himself to adorning that wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was vast and broad, surpassing and uniquely wonderful, established eternal, without decline or change.

For immeasurable kalpas he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire; he was not attached to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangible objects. He delighted only in recollecting the roots of good cultivated by all the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the tranquil conduct, far from all falsehood. Relying upon the gate of true reality, he planted the roots of all virtue, mindful not of the many sufferings.

With few desires and content, he sought only the wholesome Dharma to benefit beings. His vows never tired, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he constantly harbored compassion and forbearance. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them. He honored the Three Jewels and served teachers and elders, without any false or flattering mind.

He adorned all his conduct, and was complete in all standards of deportment. He contemplated all dharmas as illusion, and his samādhi was ever still. He well guarded his speech-karma, never ridiculing the faults of others; he well guarded his body-karma, never failing in the rules of conduct; he well guarded his mind-karma, pure and undefiled. All cities, villages, relatives, and precious treasures he held entirely without attachment. Always by the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, he taught and established sentient beings to abide in the supreme, true Way.

Because of the accomplishment of such roots of good, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures spontaneously arose and responded. Sometimes he was a householder or a wealthy elder, of noble lineage and high rank; sometimes a noble warrior, a king, or a wheel-turning sage-king; sometimes the lord of the sixth desire heaven, up to the Brahma king. At the abodes of all Buddhas he paid respect and made offerings, without ever a break. Such merits cannot be fully told.
From his body and mouth there constantly issued immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like
(zhān)

sandalwood and utpala flowers, whose fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his appearance and marks were dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly issued inexhaustible treasures and ornaments of adornment, the supreme articles for all needs, benefiting and delighting sentient beings. By these causes, he could cause immeasurable beings all to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

The Buddha told Ānanda: The Bhiksu Dharmakara, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulated merit and virtue immeasurably, boundlessly. In all dharmas he attained mastery, beyond the comprehension of speech and discrimination. The vows he had made were fully accomplished; he truly abode, complete in adornment, in a Buddha-land vast in majestic virtue and pure.

Ānanda, hearing what the Buddha said, addressed the World-Honored One: “The bodhisattva Dharmakara who attained bodhi—is he a Buddha of the past, or of the future? Or is he now present in another world?”

The World-Honored One answered: “That Tathagata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; he is unborn and unceasing, not in the past, present, or future. Only because he fulfills his vows to save beings, he is now in the West, a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands away, in a world named the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Dharmakara became a Buddha, named Amitābha. Since he attained Buddhahood, now ten kalpas have passed. Now he is present and speaks the Dharma, with an assembly of immeasurable, countless bodhisattvas and sravakas respectfully surrounding him.”

blocks.text: 10. All Making the Vow to Become a Buddha

inline.s: The Buddha spoke of how Amitābha Buddha, as a bodhisattva, obtained these vows. At that time the crown prince Ajatasatru and five hundred sons of elders, hearing it, all greatly rejoiced. Each took a golden flower-canopy, and together they came before the Buddha and paid homage. Having offered the canopies upon the Buddha, they withdrew and sat in a place apart to listen to the sutra, and in their hearts made the wish: “May we, when we become Buddhas, be just like Amitābha Buddha.”

The Buddha, knowing this, told the monks: “This prince and the others shall in the future become Buddhas. In past lives they dwelt on the bodhisattva path and, through countless kalpas, made offerings to forty kotis of Buddhas. In the time of Kasyapa Buddha they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me, and we meet again.” At that the monks, hearing the Buddha’s words, all rejoiced on their behalf.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, immeasurable merits are fully adorned. There is forever no name of the many sufferings, calamities, evil destinies, or mara afflictions. Nor is there any difference of the four seasons, cold or heat, or rain and gloom. It is peaceful and harmonious, blissful beyond compare.”

Its ground has no sea, but has rivers. There are no hills, pits, thorns, gravel, or mountains of iron, Sumeru, or earth and stone. Only from the natural seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, conch
(chē qú)
, and agate—is the ground formed, broad and level, without limit. Subtle and marvelously lovely, pure and adorned, it surpasses all the worlds of the ten directions.”
Ānanda, having heard this, addressed the World-Honored One: “If that land has no Mount Sumeru, upon what do the four heavenly kings and the Trayastrimsa heaven rely?”
The Buddha told Ānanda: “The Yama, Tusita, and up to the form and formless realms, the heavens—upon what do they rely?”
Ānanda replied: “It is due to inconceivable karmic power.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “This inconceivable karma—can you know it? The retribution of your own body is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is also inconceivable; the good roots of sentient beings are inconceivable; the sacred power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. The beings of that land, through the power of merit and virtue, abide in the stage of karma, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, are able to be thus.”

Ānanda replied: “Karmic cause and retribution are inconceivable! In this teaching I am truly without doubt. Only for the sake of future beings, to break through the net of doubt, do I raise this question.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Amitābha Buddha’s majestic light is supremely honored, first of all, beyond the reach of all the Buddhas of the ten directions. It universally illuminates the Buddha-lands of the East, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and so too the South, the West, the North, the four intermediate quarters, above and below. The lights of the Buddhas may illuminate one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand. Only Amitābha Buddha’s light universally shines upon immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.”

As to how far or near the lights of the Buddhas shine, this was determined by the vows and merits they made when seeking the Way as bodhisattvas, whether great or small. When they became Buddhas, each obtained what he had sought.

Amitābha Buddha’s light is excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand kotis of times. It is the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, also the Buddha of Boundless Light, of Unobstructed Light, of Incomparable Light; also the Light of Wisdom, the Light of Constantly Shining, the Light of Purity, the Light of Joy, the Light of Liberation, the Light of Peace, the Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and the Light of Inconceivable.

Such light universally illuminates all the worlds in the ten directions. Beings who encounter this light have their defilements extinguished and their goodness increased; their bodies and minds become gentle. If they are in the three evil paths in places of extreme suffering, seeing this light they all gain rest, and at the end of life all attain liberation. If beings hear of this light’s majestic power and merit, and speak of it day and night with single-mindedness and without interruption, according to their wishes they shall be born in that land.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Amitābha Buddha’s lifespan is long and enduring, immeasurable. The host of bodhisattvas, sravakas, gods, and humans—their lifespan and number are likewise beyond the reach of calculation and simile.”

“Among my disciples, Mahamaudgalyayana is foremost in supernormal powers. In the three-thousand great-thousand world, all the stars and beings, in a single day and night, he knows their number. Suppose all beings in the ten directions became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of a kotis of years, each with supernormal powers like Mahamaudgalyayana. Exhausting their lives and all their intellect to calculate the measure together, of a hundred parts they would not know one; of a thousand parts, a hundred thousand parts, and even in the
(wū)
upanishada portions, they would not know one.”

“It is like the great ocean, deep and broad without bound. Suppose one took a single hair and split it into a hundred parts; with one of those parts one takes a drop of water from the ocean. Between this single drop and the ocean, which is the more? Ānanda, what Mahamaudgalyayana and the rest can know is like such a drop; what they cannot know is like the water of the ocean. Amitābha Buddha’s lifespan, and the lifespan and number of the people of that land, are likewise, beyond the reach of calculation and simile.”

blocks.text: 14. Flowers and Trees Throughout the Land

inline.s: Moreover, Ānanda, in that Land of Ultimate Bliss, immeasurable merits are fully adorned. All sorts of wondrous flowers likewise fill it, everywhere pervaded with fragrance
(fù)
. There are seven-jeweled banners set in rows. Upon these jeweled banners hang streamers and canopies and many jeweled bells, replete with a hundred thousand subtle and varied colors.
Ānanda, in that Tathagata’s land there are

many jeweled trees. Some are pure gold trees, pure silver trees, pure lapis trees, pure coral trees, pure amber trees, pure conch trees, pure agate trees, each formed solely of one treasure, not mixed with other treasures. Or there are trees of two or three treasures, up to seven treasures, made by combining them. Their trunks, stems, branches, and roots are formed of these treasures; their flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from other treasures, all various and combined.
Each row is separate; row faces row, stem watches stem, branch and leaf reach toward one another, flower and fruit correspond; their hues blaze with brilliance, too much to behold.
A net of seven treasures spreads over them, soft as katapas cotton.
A clear breeze at times rises, producing five sounds, subtle as the notes of the scale, naturally harmonized. These jeweled trees fill the whole land
, their radiance resplendent, nothing in the world can compare.”

At its enlightenment-seat there is a bodhi-tree, four million li high. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas around; its branches and leaves spread, twenty thousand li. All precious treasures spontaneously formed it. Flowers and fruits bloom in profusion, their light shining everywhere. There are also red, green, blue, and white manis, the king of treasures, serving as its garlands. Cloud-gathered jeweled chains adorn its jeweled pillars. Golden bells and chimes
(duó)
hang throughout its branches.”

“A precious, wondrous net is spread over it. A hundred thousand myriad colors adorn one another; immeasurable light and radiance shine without end; all its adornments appear as fitting. A gentle breeze moves, blowing its branches and leaves, drawing forth immeasurable sounds of the wondrous Dharma. The sound flows and spreads to all Buddha-lands. Pure and clear, poignant and brilliant, subtle and harmonious—among the sounds of the ten directions it is foremost.”

“If beings look upon the bodhi-tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect its merits, they shall all attain the six faculties pure and clear, without afflictions, abiding in non-regression until they reach the Buddha Way. Moreover, by seeing that tree, they obtain three kinds of patient acceptance: first, acceptance of sounds; second, acceptance of compliance; third, acceptance of the unproduced Dharma.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “In such a Buddha-land, flowers, fruits, and trees work as Buddha-work for the many beings. All this is through Amitābha Buddha’s majestic power, his primal vow-power, his power of fulfilled vows, and his clear, firm, and ultimate vow-power.”
Moreover, the lecture halls and residences, the towers
guàn

and railings, are likewise all formed spontaneously of the seven treasures; there are also white pearls and mani gems strung in network, exceedingly luminous and wondrous. The palaces where the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.

Some there are on the ground explaining the sutra or reciting it; some receiving it and listening to it; some walking in meditation on the ground, contemplating the Way and sitting in meditation; some in the sky explaining, reciting, receiving, and listening; some walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation.

Some attain srotaapanna, some sakrdagamin, some anagamin, or arhatship. Those who have not attained the irreversibility do attain it. Each reflects on the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, all not without joy.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is no sea but there are rivers, crisscrossing in every direction, with golden sand spread over their beds. In width they are perhaps ten yojanas, twenty, or thirty yojanas, up to a hundred thousand yojanas, and twelve yojanas deep.”

“The water is calm, fragrant, and clean, tasting like ambrosia, endowed with eight qualities: first, clear; second, cool; third, sweet; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk it removes hunger, thirst, and countless other ills; eighth, when drunk it is certain to nourish the faculties and the four great elements, increasing all manner of supreme and excellent roots of good.”

“There are famous flowers floating down with the stream. A gentle breeze stirring, all sorts of fragrance are produced. On both banks grow sandalwood trees, heavenly mandarava flowers, utpala flowers,
padma flowers, kumuda flowers

, and pundarika flowers; their long branches and dense leaves intertwine over the river, blooming and bearing fruit, their fragrant brilliance a delight. Hosts of beings sport and play, coming and going as they please. Some wade into the river to bathe
(zhuó)
and romp. Deep or shallow, cold or warm, all conform to people’s wishes. There are heavenly fragrances that scatter their scent with the wind
(fù)

“The lecture halls and residences, and the dwellings where the bodhisattvas and arhats live, have bathing pools within and without, on all sides; either ten yojanas, or twenty, thirty, up to a hundred thousand yojanas, equal in length and breadth. The golden pool has silver sand at its bottom; the silver pool, golden sand; the crystal pool, lapis sand; the lapis pool, crystal sand; the coral pool, amber sand; the amber pool, coral sand; the conch pool, agate sand; the agate pool, conch sand; the white jade pool, purple-gold sand; the purple-gold pool, white-jade sand. On the shores grow sandalwood trees, their flowers and leaves hanging and spreading, their fragrance pervasively diffused. The water of the eight qualities fills them. When one wishes to bathe, he enters the pool and bathes. If he wishes the water to reach his feet, his knees, his waist, his armpits, or his neck; or wishes to pour it over his body; or wishes it cold, warm, swift, or slow—the water follows every wish, opening the spirit and delighting the body.”

“Amitābha Buddha’s jeweled pool is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. The natural seven treasures are combined to form it. The sand at its bottom is all white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani gems. The water of the eight qualities is pure as if without form; gems and sand shine through it, and there is no depth it does not illume. Gentle ripples slowly turn, pouring into one another. On its shores are sandalwood trees, auspicious fruit trees
, heavenly mandarava flowers

, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kunuda flowers, and pundarika flowers—fresh flowers and great fruit, ever blooming in splendor, their light shining, of utmost beauty. Long branches and dense leaves interweave over the water. All sorts of fragrance are produced, beyond all comparison, and the perfume drifts along the stream.”

“The waves raise immeasurable, subtle sounds; one hears the sound of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; the sound of the perfections; the sound of stilling and quiescence; the sound of the unborn and unceasing; the sound of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses; or the sound of no self-nature, no fabrication, no self; the sound of great compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and giving; the sound of ambrosia sprinkling the crown and receiving the prediction. Having heard such manifold sounds, the mind becomes pure and without discriminations, upright and equal, ripening all roots of good. Whatever one hears accords with the Dharma. Those who wish to hear, hear it alone
(zhé)
; what they do not wish to hear, they hear nothing of it. Never do they regress from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
In that Land of Ultimate Bliss,
the bodhisattvas, sravakas, gods, and humans, with wisdom lofty and clear, supernormal powers thorough and penetrating, are all of one kind,
free of any distinguishing marks.
Their countenances upright, their forms and colors subtle, surpassing and rare in the world, neither gods nor humans, they all receive a naturally pure and ethereal body, a body without limit.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Consider the poor beggars of the world: standing beside a king, could their faces and forms be compared? If a king were compared to a wheel-turning sage-king, he would be base and ugly, just as that beggar beside the king. The wheel-turning sage-king, foremost in majestic marks, compared to the king of Trayastrimsa heaven, would be yet more ugly and inferior. Even the king of Trayastrimsa, compared to the king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations, does not come close, not by a hundred thousand times. The king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations, compared to the bodhisattvas and sravakas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in luminous countenance and hue, does not come near them, not by a crore of times.”

The palaces they dwell in, their clothing, food, and drink, are like those of the king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations. As for their majestic virtue, rank, supernormal powers, and transformations, all the gods and humans cannot be compared to them, not by a hundred thousand myriads of kotis.
Ānanda, you should know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha has such accumulated merit and adornment, inconceivable!

Moreover, all beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether already born, now born, or to be born, all obtain such wondrous forms and bodies. Their appearance is upright and dignified, their merit and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and bright, their supernormal powers free and spontaneous. All manner of enjoyments are entirely abundant. Palaces, clothing, ornaments, flowers, streamers, canopies, and all furnishings of adornment, whatever they desire, all appear as one wishes.

When one wishes to eat, jeweled bowls of the seven treasures spontaneously appear before him, and the hundred flavors of food spontaneously fill them. Though there is this food, in truth there is none who eats it. Only seeing its colors and smelling its fragrance, one is nourished by thought; strength and vitality increase, without any waste. The body and mind become gentle and soft, without attachment to any taste. When the meal is over it vanishes, and in due time appears again.
There are also superb garments of many treasures, crowns, sashes, necklaces, with immeasurable light and a hundred thousand subtle colors, all complete and spontaneously upon the body.

The dwellings they dwell in have forms and colors to delight the heart. A jeweled net is spread over them, and jeweled bells are hung. Wondrous and marvelously rare, adorned all about, their brilliance dazzling, utterly majestic and beautiful. Towers, railings, halls, and chambers, broad or narrow, square or round, great or small, some in the sky, some on the ground, all pure, peaceful, and still, subtle and blissful. They appear before the mind’s call, none lacking.

“In that Buddha-land, at every mealtime, a natural virtuous wind gently and joyfully rises, blowing the jeweled nets and the many jeweled trees, producing subtle sounds that expound suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self, and the many perfections, and spreading abroad ten thousand kinds of gentle, elegant virtue-fragrance. Those who hear it find their dusty defilements and habitual stains naturally cease. The wind touching their bodies makes them peaceful and harmonious, like a monk who has attained the cessation samādhi.”

“It moreover blows the seven-jeweled groves and trees, sending the wafting flowers into heaps, with all sorts of colors and lights filling the Buddha-land. In order of color they are laid without confusion, soft and bright, like katapas cotton. When one sets foot upon them, the foot sinks to four fingers’ depth, and as the foot lifts they rise back to their former state. After the mealtime the flowers vanish of themselves, and the great earth is pure. In due seasons it rains new flowers, again covering it everywhere, just as before, and so six times.”

Moreover, many lotus flowers of treasure fill the whole world. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand kotis of petals. Their light is immeasurable; the colors are countless. Blue hues emit blue light, white hues emit white light; dark, yellow, coral, and purple, their light and color likewise. There are also immeasurable superb treasures, a hundred thousand mani gems, adorning the rare and wondrous, shining upon sun and moon.

“The size of those lotuses is either half a yojana, or one, two, three, four, up to a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower there issue thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of rays of light. Within each ray there appear thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of Buddhas, their bodies purple-gold, their marks and excellences surpassing and rare. Each of these Buddhas again emits a hundred thousand rays of light, and universally for the ten directions speaks the subtle Dharma. Such Buddhas each establish immeasurable beings upon the Buddha’s right Way.”

All those reborn in the worlds of the ten directions are spontaneously born by transformation within the lotus flowers of the seven-jeweled pools. They all receive a pure, ethereal body, a body without limit. They never hear the names of the three evil paths’ evil afflictions and miseries. If those names do not even exist, how much less the actual suffering? There is only the sound of natural happiness. Therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: 22. Dwelling in the Stage of Rightness

inline.s: Moreover, Ānanda, that Buddha-land has no darkness, no fire-light, no sun, moon, or stars
yào

, no appearance of day or night, no name of months, years, or kalpas, and no attachment to homes and families. In every place, having neither markers nor names, neither grasping nor rejecting nor discriminating, they receive only purity and the utmost happiness.

If good men or good women, whether already born or to be born there, all dwell in the stage of rightness, they will certainly realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why? Because those in the stage of wrongness and the undecided stage cannot understand the causes that establish that stage.

blocks.text: 23. Praises of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions

inline.s: Moreover, Ānanda, in the worlds of the East as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each of these worlds, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges each put forth the broad and long tongue, emit immeasurable light, and speak truthful words, praising the inconceivable merits of Amitābha Buddha. The Buddhas of the South, West, and North, in Ganges-sand worlds, praise him likewise. In the four intermediate quarters, above and below, in Ganges-sand worlds, the Buddhas praise him likewise.

Why is this? Because they wish all beings of other lands, hearing that Buddha’s name, to give rise to a pure mind, recollect, receive, and uphold it, and take refuge and make offerings. Even those able to give rise to a single thought of pure faith, with all their good roots, sincerely dedicating them, wishing to be born in that land—according to their vows they shall all be born there, never regressing, up to supreme right enlightenment.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “In the worlds of the ten directions, among the gods and humans, those who with sincere heart wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.”

“The highest grade are those who, abandoning home and desire, become sramanas, give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitābha Buddha, cultivate all merits, and wish to be born in that land. Such beings, at the end of their lives, have Amitābha Buddha and the great assembly appear before them, and then follow that Buddha to be born in his land. In the lotus flower of the seven-jeweled pool they are spontaneously born by transformation, abiding in non-regression, with wisdom brave and keen, supernormal powers free and spontaneous. Therefore, Ānanda, beings who wish to see Amitābha Buddha in this life should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi, cultivate merit and virtue, and wish to be born in that land.”

“The middle grade are those who, though unable to practice as sramanas or greatly cultivate merits, should give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitābha Buddha, and cultivate some good. They observe the fasts and precepts, raise stupas and images, provide meals for sramanas, hang streamers and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense, and with this dedicate the merit, wishing to be born in that land. At death Amitābha Buddha transforms a body, with light and marks completely like the true Buddha, and with the great assembly appears before them. They follow the transformed Buddha and are born in his land, abiding in non-regression; their merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.”

“The lowest grade are those who, even if unable to do all the merits, should give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitābha Buddha, up to ten recollections, wishing to be born in his land. And there are beings who, hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice in faith and delight, without doubt, and even with a single thought recollect that Buddha, with a most sincere heart, wishing to be born in his land. At death they see Amitābha Buddha in a dream, and are also able to be reborn there; their merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.”

Moreover, Ānanda, if a good man or good woman hears this scripture, receives, upholds, recites, copies, and makes offerings to it, continuing day and night, seeking birth in that land; gives rise to the bodhi mind, upholds all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefits sentient beings, and gives to them all the good roots he has done to bring them peace and joy; recollects Amitābha Buddha and his land—such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha’s form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never regresses.

Moreover, Ānanda, if beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditation or fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should do good. That is: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not sexual misconduct; fourth, not false speech; fifth, not idle talk; sixth, not harsh speech; seventh, not slander; eighth, not greed; ninth, not anger; tenth, not foolishness. Thus day and night reflecting upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha’s manifold merits and manifold adornments, with a sincere heart take refuge, bow, and make offerings. Such a person, at death, without fright or fear, with mind not inverted, is then born in that Buddha-land.”

If one is occupied with many affairs and cannot leave home, and has not the leisure to greatly observe the fasts and precepts and keep a single mind pure, then, when he has spare time, let him rectify body and mind, abandon desire and put away sorrow, and with a loving heart be vigorous. He should not be angry or envious, nor gluttonous
(tiè)
or stingy
(qiān)
. He must not later regret, nor harbor doubt.

“He should be filial, sincere, and true. He should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and that doing good brings blessings. He should uphold such teachings and not fail in them. Thinking and pondering deeply, wishing to attain liberation, day and night constantly recollecting, wishing to be reborn in Amitābha Buddha’s pure Buddha-land—those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at death shall all be reborn in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.”

All those reborn there attain irreversibility, possess the true golden-colored body with thirty-two marks, and shall all become Buddhas. In whatever Buddha-land they wish to become a Buddha, it follows the wishes of their mind. According to their vigor, seeking the Way morning and evening without rest, they shall surely obtain it, without failing their vows.
Ānanda, because of the benefit and advantage of this, in immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless worlds, all the Tathagatas together praise all the merits of Amitābha Buddha.

blocks.text: 26. Paying Homage to the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: Moreover, Ānanda, the hosts of bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to pay homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, each with incense, flowers, banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies, go to that Buddha’s abode. They respectfully make offerings, hear and receive the Dharma, proclaim the Way and its transformation, and praise the adorning merits of that Buddha-land.
At that moment the World-Honored One spoke a verse:
The Buddha-lands of the East, numberless as the Ganges’ sands; hosts of bodhisattvas, like Ganges sands, go to pay homage to Immeasurable Life.
South, West, North, the four angles, above and below, likewise; all with a reverent heart offer precious and wondrous gifts.
They pour forth harmonious and elegant tones, singing the praises of the most supreme and honored One, penetrating to his transcendental wisdom, entering his deep Dharma-gate.
Hearing the name of the Buddha’s holy virtue, they gain peace and great advantage; among all manner of offerings, they diligently cultivate without slack or weariness.

Beholding that supremely wondrous land, subtle and beyond thought, its merits universally adorn it, no Buddha-land can compare; thereupon they raise the unsurpassed mind, and wish quickly to accomplish bodhi.

At that the Measureless Honored One smiled, and showed his golden face. Light issued from his mouth, universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions; the light returned and circled the Buddha, then entered his crown, making three rounds.
The bodhisattvas seeing this light straightway attained the stage of non-regression; all the assembly at that time rejoiced with one another.
The Buddha’s voice thundered like the Brahma bell, and with the eight tones he uttered the wondrous sound:
“The right-minded ones come from the ten directions; I know all their vows—they seek to adorn the pure land, and are to be predicted to become Buddhas.
Realizing all dharmas as like dream, illusion, and echo, they fulfill all the wondrous vows, and shall surely accomplish such a land.”

“Knowing the land as like a shadow or image, they ever raise the heart of great vows; they carry the bodhisattva path to perfection, complete the root of all merit, cultivate the supreme bodhi-conduct, and are to be predicted to become Buddhas.”
Thoroughly penetrating the nature of all dharmas, all empty and without self, they single-mindedly seek the pure Buddha-land, and will surely accomplish such a world.

Hearing the Dharma, they delight in receiving and practicing it, and attain the place of purity; they will surely receive the prophecy from the Measureless Honored Ones and accomplish right enlightenment.
The boundless and supreme land is the power of the Buddha's original vows; hearing the name and wishing to be reborn there, they naturally reach the state of non-retrogression.

The bodhisattvas bring forth the supreme vow, wishing their own land be without difference, universally mindful to save all beings; each brings forth the bodhi mind, abandoning the body of the cycle of rebirth, and all cause them to reach the other shore.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: The bodhisattvas of the Land of Bliss, relying on the Buddha's majestic power, in the space of a single meal, go again to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas. Flowers, incense, canopies, and banners, the offerings, appear as soon as they are thought of, all manifesting in their hands. Wondrous, fine, and extraordinary, not of this world, they present them to the Buddhas and the bodhisattva assemblies.

The flowers they scatter, in the sky, unite into one flower. The flowers all face downward, round and complete on every side, and transform into flower canopies. With a hundred and a thousand lights and colors, each color with a different fragrance, the fragrance pervades everywhere. The smaller canopies cover ten yojanas, and so multiplied, until they cover the entire three thousand great thousand worlds. Following the order of their going, in sequence they transform and vanish. If new flowers are not scattered again, the former scattered flowers never fall. In the sky, together they play heavenly music, and with subtle tones sing and praise the Buddha's virtues.

In a short while, they return to their own land, all gathering in the seven-jeweled hall. Amitābha Buddha broadly proclaims the great teaching, and expounds the wondrous Dharma. None do not rejoice, and their minds comprehend the Way.

At once a fragrant wind blows the seven-jeweled trees, producing a music of five sounds. Measureless wonderful flowers, scattered in all directions with the wind, naturally make offerings, unceasingly like this. All the devas bring
ji

a hundred and a thousand flowers and incense, and ten thousand kinds of music, to make offerings to that Buddha and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and sravakas. Going and coming, they are cheerful and happy. This is all due to the power of Amitābha Buddha's original vows, and because they once offered to the Tathagatas, their roots of goodness continuing without deficiency or loss, because of their good cultivation, good taking in, and good accomplishment.

The Buddha told Ānanda: The assemblies of bodhisattvas in that Buddha-land all clearly see and thoroughly hear the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. The devas and people, and the flying and creeping creatures, the good and evil intentions of their minds, what their mouths wish to say, when they will be liberated and attain the Way and be reborn, all these are known beforehand.

The assemblies of sravakas in that Buddha-land have body-light of one fathom, while the bodhisattvas' light illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and foremost, whose majestic power and light universally illumine the three thousand great thousand worlds.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?

The Buddha said: One is named Avalokitesvara, and one is named Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas, in the Sahā world, cultivated the bodhisattva path, and were reborn in that land, always dwelling at the side of Amitābha Buddha. If they wish to go to the measureless Buddha-places of the ten directions, they arrive as their minds wish. They now dwell in this world, doing great benefit and joy. The good men and good women of the world, if in sudden calamity or terror, need only take refuge in Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and none fail to be liberated.

Moreover, Ānanda, in that Buddha-land, all the bodhisattvas, present and future, will all certainly reach the state of one-life continuation. Only those who, because of great vows, enter the realm of birth and death to save all beings, and roar the lion's roar. Having put on
huan
the great armor
zhou

, they adorn themselves with the merit of the vast vows. Though born in the five defilements of the evil world, they appear the same there, until reaching Buddhahood they do not fall into evil destinies; in every place of birth, they always remember their past lives.

Amitābha Buddha, intending to liberate the classes of beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in the Land of Bliss and attain the Way of nirvāṇa, causing them all to become Buddhas. Having become Buddhas, they in turn, in the worlds of the ten directions, teach each other, and liberate each other. Thus turning and turning, it can never be reckoned.

In the worlds of the ten directions, the sravakas, bodhisattvas, and all classes of beings born in the Land of Bliss, who attain the Way of nirvāṇa and are to become Buddhas, cannot be numbered. In that Buddha-land, it is ever as one Dharma, not increasing in number. Why is this so? Just as the great sea is the king of waters, and all the waters flow into the sea—does the water of the great sea increase?

The Buddha-lands in the eight directions, above and below, are countless. The Land of Bliss, long-lasting and vast, bright and glorious and joyful, is the most supremely outstanding. This is from the time when he was a bodhisattva, seeking the Way according to his vow, the fruits accumulated through merit. Amitābha Buddha's grace and virtue spread to the eight directions, above and below, without end or limit, deep, vast, and measureless, beyond all words.

blocks.text: Chapter 30: The Practice of the Bodhisattvas

inline.s: Moreover, Ānanda, in that Buddha-land, all the bodhisattvas, in concentration, wisdom, supernatural powers, and majestic virtue, are all perfect. The Buddha's secret treasury, they understand to the ultimate. They tame their faculties, and body and mind become soft and gentle. They enter deep right wisdom, with no remaining habits. Following the Buddha's practice, the seven limbs of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

With eloquence and perfect retention, they are free and unobstructed. They skillfully understand the boundless expedient means of the world. Their words are true and sincere, penetrating deeply into the flavor of meaning. They save all beings, expounding the right Dharma. Without form, without exertion, without bondage, without liberation. Without all discrimination, far from inversion. Regarding what they receive and use, they are without any grasping.

Roaming throughout the Buddha-lands, without love or aversion. Without a thought of seeking or not seeking, nor a thought of self and other, of opposition or resentment. Why? Because those bodhisattvas have great compassion and a heart of benefit toward all sentient beings. Renouncing all attachment, they accomplish measureless merit.

With unobstructed wisdom, they understand dharmas as thusness. Skillfully knowing arising and ceasing, the expedient means of sound. Not delighting in worldly talk, they delight in right discourse. Knowing all dharmas are all empty and still. The body-born afflictions and the remaining two, both are exhausted. In the three worlds, cultivating diligently and equally, they reach the ultimate one vehicle and arrive at the other shore.

Decisively severing the net of doubt, they realize nothing-attained. With the wisdom of expedient means, they grow in understanding. From the beginning, abiding in supernatural powers, they attain the way of the one vehicle, no longer relying on others for their awakening.

Their wisdom is vast and deep, like the great sea. Their bodhi is lofty and broad, like the Sumeru mountain. Their own majestic light surpasses the sun and moon. Their minds are white and pure, like the snow mountains. Their patience is like the earth, all things equal. Pure like water, washing away all dust and defilement. Blazing like fire, burning the fuel of affliction. Unattached like wind, without any obstruction.

The Dharma-sound roars like thunder, awakening the not yet awakened. Raining the nectar of Dharma, to moisten sentient beings. Vast like empty space, through great and equal compassion. Like a pure lotus, free from defilement. Like the nyagrodha tree, providing great shade. Like the vajra pestle, destroying false attachments. Like the iron walled mountain, which the host of demons and non-Buddhists cannot move.

Their minds are upright and true, skillfully and decisively. Discussing the Dharma without weariness, seeking the Dharma without fatigue. Their precepts like crystal, bright and pure within and without. What they say causes the assembly to rejoice and submit. Beating the Dharma-drum, erecting the Dharma-banner, lighting the sun of wisdom, destroying the darkness of ignorance. Pure, gentle, and harmonious, still, settled, and clear-sighted. As great guides, they tame self and others. Guiding all beings, they abandon all attachment, forever separate from the three defilements, and sport in supernatural powers.

Through the power of conditions and vows, they give rise to roots of goodness, subdue all the hosts of demons, and reverently serve the Buddhas. As the bright lamps of the world, the supreme fields of blessings. Supremely auspicious, worthy of offerings. Brilliant and joyous, valiant and fearless, with bodies adorned with the marks of beauty. Merit and eloquence, perfectly adorned, with nothing to equal them. Always praised by all the Buddhas together. They perfect the bodhisattva's perfections, and always abide in the samādhis of non-arising and non-ceasing. Their practice fills the enlightenment-sites, far beyond the realm of the two vehicles.

Ānanda, I have now briefly spoken of the true and real merit of the bodhisattvas born in that Land of Bliss, all being thus. If I were to speak at length, even a hundred thousand million aeons could not exhaust it.

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the devas and people: The sravakas and bodhisattvas of the Land of Measureless Life, their merit and wisdom cannot be spoken of, and again their land is so wondrous, peaceful, happy, and pure as this. Why not diligently do good, and be mindful of the naturalness of the Way?

Going out and coming in to make offerings, contemplating the sutras and practicing the Way, delighting and long practicing. With fierce and vigorous wisdom, the mind does not turn back, and the intention is never slack. Though outwardly slow and relaxed, inwardly alone, swift and urgent. Vast and empty, just attaining the middle. Within and without corresponding, naturally dignified and ordered. Contracted, upright, and straight, body and mind clean and pure.

Without love or greed, the will is settled and steady. Without increase or decrease, seeking the Way in harmony and uprightness. Not erring toward the crooked, following the sutras and their injunctions. Not daring to stumble, as if on the carpenter's line. All devoted to the Way, vast without other thoughts. Without sorrow or worry, naturally effortless. Empty and without establishment, serene and without desire.

Making good vows, seeking them with all one's heart. Containing compassion and kindness, all rites and righteousness united, embracing within and without, passing over to liberation. Naturally guarding and holding, truly, truly white and pure, with the supreme vow, pure, settled, and happy.

Once one reaches clarity and thorough understanding, naturally the natural state within the natural state, the natural having its root. Naturally forming five lights, the five lights transforming into nine colors, the stars
(shen)

circling and turning, hundreds and thousands of changes, the most supreme naturalness.
